attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: The checkable core is a present-tense claim that OpenAI is the majority of compute demand at effectively every provider. The 'probably fund it' part is hedged, and the contract rightly leaves it unscored.

contract.note: Limiting this to AI compute, fixing the provider set from the post itself and using the latest quarter before publication (Apr–Jun 2026) is an ordinary reading. It also correctly refuses to treat revenue or backlog as compute demand.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q4 FY26 disclosure covers commercial RPO and cloud revenue mix, not OpenAI's share of AI compute demand. It uses a different denominator, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no provider-level figures for OpenAI's share of AI compute demand in the target quarter. The only item is Microsoft's revenue and RPO data, which uses a different metric. The evidence neither shows nor refutes a majority share at effectively every provider.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: The consequences follow from OpenAI dying. 'Its collapse' could grammatically mean SoftBank's, but either way the antecedent is a collapse that has not happened. 'Will guarantee' is firm language.

contract.note: Assessing only after a documented collapse is fair. The readings of existential threat and massive guidance changes are ordinary.

evidence.note: SoftBank's 1 Oct 2026 release says it completed its $30B follow-on investment, which suggests OpenAI had not collapsed. It is evidence on the antecedent, not the outcome. The packet mentions an e1 that is not included, but the result does not depend on it.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast whose antecedent, OpenAI's collapse, had not happened by the evaluation date. No post-collapse solvency or guidance evidence can exist yet, so under policy it is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense claim that further rounds are near-impossible without huge backers who show increasing strain. The normalised wording keeps both parts.

contract.note: The plain reading (practical dependence on giant backers at the scale discussed, as of Aug 18) is ordinary. But 'near-impossible' and 'massive entities' have no thresholds, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: The March round was anchored by Amazon, NVIDIA and SoftBank, with many other institutions taking part. It shows reliance on strategic investors but not whether alternatives were unavailable in August. It is from an earlier period.
Amazon's trailing-twelve-month free cash flow turned to a $7.6B outflow on higher AI capex while operating cash flow rose. That is ambiguous as financing strain, and it covers one backer only.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet shows that a large round without giant backers was or was not feasible in August 2026. Amazon's negative free cash flow is partial context on one backer. Broad participation in the March round does not refute dependence. The evidence settles neither part.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: A firm necessity claim ('will have to') tied to survival up to 'then', which in context means the projected 2030 turn to positive free cash flow. 'Profitable' slightly loosens the free-cash-flow framing, and the contract notes this.

contract.note: Annual external financing received over 2026–2030, with leeway for 'basically every year', is a fair, ordinary reading. It rightly says raising the money alone does not prove it was necessary.

evidence.note: The $122B committed in March 2026 is consistent with the range for one year. But it is committed capital, not proceeds, and it does not show what was needed to survive.

reviews.rationale: The horizon runs to 2030 and has not passed. Whether OpenAI survives through the period, the antecedent, is unknown. No conclusive early event is in the packet. Under policy the claim is not scored yet.
